criteria.note: The TL;DR answers the 'celiac travel korea' intent inside the first 200 words — Korea is doable with prep, named Tier 1 anchors, the allergy phrase, and the store baseline — and a dedicated 'If You're Celiac, Start Here' block follows immediately.

Title is 55 chars with the rendered ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix, description is ~146 chars, keyword present in both, and the description adds four distinct content promises rather than restating the title.

Headings are descriptive rather than labelled ('What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle', 'The One Phrase That Actually Works', Tier 1/2/3), and skimming them alone reproduces the argument.
Seven distinct internal destinations (restaurants roundup, bakeries, phrases, BBQ guide, label guide, snacks, About), each placed where a reader would actually want the deeper piece.
All five frontmatter Q/As are reproduced verbatim in the visible body and each is supported by a corresponding body section, so the markup matches rendered content and each answer stands alone.

Restaurant and label sections carry real dated specifics, but the single most-repeated experiential claim is a composite with no shop, neighbourhood, or month, and the piece never narrates a first-hand failure of its own method.
criteria.evidence_quote: During our first year back (2025–26), I asked bakery owners under "Gluten-Free" neon signs about their flour ratio and was told cheerfully: "Oh, 90% rice flour, 10% wheat flour."

criteria.note: Hangul with romanisation throughout (어묵/eomuk, 밀떡, 쌀떡, 뻥튀기), named products (Poca Chip Original vs Onion, 참쌀설병 pink vs green, 고래사), and a citable regulation clause — all checkable by a reader.

Three sources, each linked with a retrieval or publication date: the 시행규칙 별표 2 text 'in force as of August 2026', Orion's own product page 're-verified August 2026', and a blogger roundup 'published October 2023' explicitly downgraded to a lead.

The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish ('our standard is NCGS, and we can't audit a kitchen', the retracted GFCO claim, the year-old franchise call) and carries no undisclosed commercial links.

findings.quote: During our first year back (2025–26), I asked bakery owners under "Gluten-Free" neon signs about their flour ratio and was told cheerfully: "Oh, 90% rice flour, 10% wheat flour."
findings.why: This anecdote is the load-bearing evidence for the whole 'marketing trap' argument and it is repeated three times (TL;DR, body, FAQ 5), yet it names no shop, no neighbourhood and no month, and the plural 'bakery owners' turns it into a composite rather than an observed event. The adjacent online-loaf story likewise names no vendor. Elsewhere the article anchors claims precisely (237 closed summer 2026, franchise call summer 2025, pink vs green packet mid-2026), which makes the gap conspicuous rather than stylistic.
findings.fix: Anchor one of the two anecdotes: shop name or at minimum street/neighbourhood plus month and year, in the singular ('In November 2025 a bakery on X-ro in Y-dong told me…'). Separately, add one short first-hand failure — a meal where the reconfirmation script failed or a label read wrong, with what happened afterwards — since 'mistakes we've made (and still sometimes make)' is currently asserted but never instantiated.

findings.quote: Everything below is field-tested at my wife's NCGS standard — your standard is stricter.
findings.why: Handled with real integrity, but a reader arriving on 'celiac travel korea' wants celiac-safe venues, and every Tier 2 and Tier 3 recommendation is stamped as NCGS-tested only. The query's intent is answered early, so no point is withheld, but the page's competitive weakness against a celiac-specific competitor is that its evidence base does not meet the standard its keyword names.
findings.fix: For each Tier 2 entry, add one celiac-specific verification line where you have it — dedicated fryer yes/no, separate prep surface, flour used on site — even if the answer is 'we asked and they could not tell us'. That converts the disclosure from a caveat into differentiated data.

findings.quote: Only commit to dedicated GF bakeries like monil2 house and Cafe Rebirth.
findings.why: The FAQ question is specifically about buying gluten-free bread, but the body describes Cafe Rebirth as a cafe whose 'seasonal fruit cakes are the signature' and never establishes that it sells bread. If this Q/A surfaces as a rich result it points a bread-seeking reader at a venue the body does not support for bread.
findings.fix: Either add a clause to the Cafe Rebirth entry confirming it bakes bread, or narrow the FAQ answer to 'dedicated GF bakeries like monil2 house' and mention Cafe Rebirth as a cake/dessert stop.

findings.why: Four preambles run before the first substantive section: the update note, TL;DR, the celiac rules block, and this table of contents, followed by another narrative intro. The TOC restates headings the reader has already been given twice in compressed form, pushing 'What Korean Food Actually Looks Like' well down the page and diluting the strong opening.
findings.fix: Drop the manual TOC in favour of an auto-generated sidebar, or merge it into the TL;DR. The celiac five-rule block already functions as the navigational summary.

findings.quote: For the full writeup see our [gluten-free restaurants roundup](/blog/gluten-free-restaurants-seoul).
findings.why: Every internal link points at another blog post; none point at the site's own place detail pages, which carry Restaurant JSON-LD and address data. Linking blog to directory would pass relevance to the pages best positioned to win local queries and would give the reader the taxi-address card at the moment they are deciding to go.
findings.fix: Link each Tier 1 and Tier 2 venue name to its /place/[slug] page on first mention, keeping the roundup links as the 'full writeup' secondary.

findings.quote: She reacts badly to gluten — vomiting, bloating, diarrhea — but she tolerates trace amounts that would make a celiac person seriously ill.
findings.why: The clinical distinction between NCGS and celiac disease is what justifies every 'apply stricter standards' instruction on a page targeting celiac readers, yet it carries no attribution. The article's three dated sources cover a labelling regulation and two snack lists; nothing medical is cited on a page aimed at a medical population.
findings.fix: Cite one dated clinical or regulatory source for the celiac threshold — the Codex 20 mg/kg standard already confirmed in your own research, or a coeliac association page with its publication date — and link it at this sentence and at the 'low-gluten' warning.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is either linked to a source, attributed to a dated call/visit, or explicitly marked as the author's own field observation; a small number of convenience-store generalisations are asserted without any source or attribution.
criteria.evidence_quote: **Packaged grilled chicken breast** (닭가슴살) — skip anything marinated in soy sauce; plain is usually safe.

criteria.note: Product names, shops, districts, prices-free figures and all dates (April 2026 publication, August 2026 update, summer 2025 franchise call, October 2023 blogger post) are checkable and internally consistent, with no invented statistic.

The piece states exactly how it knows each thing — visits, a phone call to headquarters, reading 원재료명, a manufacturer product page, a third-party blog — and states plainly what those methods cannot establish ("we can't audit a kitchen", "field notes, not a database", blogger entries "treat them as leads").

NCGS is separated from celiac disease up front and repeatedly, no absolute safety guarantee is made (even Tier 1 is hedged with "one confirming question at the counter costs nothing"), and cross-contamination is addressed at grills, fryers, shared kitchens, shared production lines and "wheat-free label is not a celiac guarantee".

Every source carries a retrieval or occurrence date and staleness is flagged where it bites — the 2025 franchise call is explicitly aged ("A year has passed since that call"), the 2023 blog roundup is demoted to "leads", and reformulation-without-notice is stated as a standing caution.

The load-bearing fact is stated correctly and twice — mandatory allergen labelling covers wheat only, with 보리 and 호밀 explicitly outside it — and the legal citation (시행규칙 별표 2, 소비자 안전을 위한 표시사항) and Korean food terms (밀떡/쌀떡, 어묵, 쌈장, 집간장, 소맥분) are all right.

The reader gets a direct link to the law text, a manufacturer allergen page, the exact Korean strings to scan for, and repeated instructions to confirm at the counter or on the packet in hand rather than trust the article.

findings.quote: **Plain yogurt** — check flavored versions; some have wheat-based thickeners.
findings.why: This is an unsourced product-category generalisation presented as fact. It errs toward caution so it will not cause gluten ingestion, but a reader cannot check where it comes from, and 'wheat-based thickeners' in yogurt is an unusual enough claim that it needs either a source or an 'in our experience' marker like the rest of the piece uses.
findings.fix: Either cite one product label where a flavoured yogurt declares 밀, or reframe as a field note: 'we've seen flavoured versions with wheat-derived thickeners — check the 원재료명 rather than assuming.'

findings.quote: A brunch spot with oatmeal pancakes and sandwiches that can be modified with GF bread swaps.
findings.why: A GF bread swap in a wheat-bread brunch kitchen is the highest cross-contamination exposure of any specific recommendation in the article, and it is the one Tier 2 entry with no local caveat — Cafe Pepper gets 'in a shared kitchen', ssaltongdak gets 'individual branches may have cross-contamination', benir gets a topping warning. The global Tier 2 and rule-4 framing covers it, but the omission is inconsistent with the article's own standard.
findings.fix: Add one clause matching the other Tier 2 entries, e.g. 'the swap is a bread substitution in a shared kitchen with wheat bread and a shared toaster — for celiac readers that is not a safe order without asking about prep surfaces.'

findings.quote: Rice-labeled products often contain wheat starch as a binder.
findings.why: 'Often' is a frequency claim with no source or observation marker, sitting in the label section where readers are being taught a rule. The direction is protective, so no safety consequence, but it is stated more firmly than the evidence offered.
findings.fix: Attribute it the way the food-category section does — 'in the packets we've flipped, wheat starch turns up as a binder often enough that the rice headline tells you nothing' — or link one example label.
